title: Algorithms, Statistics & Model Evaluation
subtitle: From the map of algorithms and applied statistics to metrics worked through with numbers, search systems and time series
deliverable: Choose the right algorithm family, calculate metrics from a confusion matrix and error tables, and judge whether the difference between two models is real.
intro: The exam does not ask you to derive algorithms. It asks: which family suits this situation, and why? Is the difference between the two models real or noise? What is the value of precision, recall, F1, MAE and nDCG in this table? Which threshold is correct given the analyst capacity available? This unit continues what the previous unit began: the map of supervised, unsupervised and specialised algorithms; the statistics an engineer needs to read results correctly; hyper-parameter tuning, model selection and interpretability; then metrics worked through with complete numbers, the design of the evaluation set, data engineering, and search, recommendation and time-series systems in production.
outcomes: Distinguish the supervised and unsupervised algorithm families by their core idea, strengths, weaknesses and the scenario signals that point to each.
Calculate precision, recall, specificity, F1 and false-positive rate from a confusion matrix, and choose a feasible threshold according to capacity and cost.
Calculate Macro-F1, Weighted-F1, MAE, RMSE, WAPE, bias, Precision@k, Recall@k, MRR and nDCG, and interpret what each one reveals.
Estimate the uncertainty in metrics using the standard error and confidence intervals, and interpret the p-value, statistical power and the pitfalls of A/B tests.
Choose a hyper-parameter tuning method, compare models on criteria that go beyond the leaderboard, and choose the interpretability technique that suits the audience.
Design an evaluation set that is representative, stratified, isolated, versioned and tied to release gates.
Design data engineering components, the search and recommendation funnel, and time-series and streaming-learning practices in production.
method: This is a unit of calculation and discrimination. In Chapter 3, redo every calculation by hand before reading the result, so that reading a confusion matrix and an error table becomes a habit that needs no thought on exam day. In the algorithm tables, memorise the “Choose when” column and the “Weaknesses” column, because distractors are usually built from a strong algorithm used in the wrong place. In statistics, practise stating the p-value in one correct sentence and calculating the approximate confidence interval; these two skills are enough to eliminate half the options in “which model is better?” questions.

chapters.title: The Algorithm Map and Domain Patterns

blocks.p: For each family: the core idea, what it does well and what it does not, and the scenario signals that point to it. The general rule: on tabular data, boosted trees are the strong default; when interpretability for regulators is a requirement, logistic regression comes first; when the data is unstructured and very large, neural networks come first.

blocks.p: A recurring trap: using t-SNE or UMAP output as features for a model, or reading the distances between clusters in them as if they were meaningful. They are visualisation tools only.

**Recommender systems** combine collaborative filtering (users who behave alike like similar items — matrix factorisation, two-tower neural models) with content-based signals (item attributes, text and image embeddings). The **cold-start problem** — new users or items with no history — is solved with content features, popularity priors and onboarding questions. Production recommenders usually work in two stages: fast candidate retrieval (approximate nearest-neighbour (ANN) search over the embeddings), then a heavier ranking model, then business rules (diversity, freshness, compliance). Offline metrics (Recall@k, nDCG) must be confirmed by live A/B tests because of feedback loops: the system only learns about what it chose to show.

**Time-series forecasting** ranges from classical statistical models (exponential smoothing, ARIMA/SARIMA) to boosted trees with lag and calendar features, to deep models for many related series. The strongest practical baseline is often the seasonal naive forecast (“same as last week”) — any model must beat it. Saudi calendar effects (Ramadan, which moves forward by about 11 days each Gregorian year, the Eids, salary day, school terms and the summer season) must be encoded explicitly, usually with Hijri-calendar features. Always validate forward in time; the metrics are MAE, RMSE, MAPE (unsafe near zero) and sMAPE/MASE.

**Ranking and search** optimise the order, not the labels: learning-to-rank with pointwise, pairwise or listwise approaches, evaluated with nDCG, MRR and Precision@k — the same metrics used for RAG retrievers.

table: Critical for scanned Arabic documents; right-to-left layout, ligatures and diacritics need Arabic-capable OCR

blocks.p: **Speech pipelines** chain automatic speech recognition (ASR), then optionally diarisation (who spoke and when), then text models. In Arabic call centres, dialect coverage is the decisive factor in accuracy.

chapters.title: Statistics, Tuning, Model Selection and Interpretability

blocks.p: Every metric computed on a sample is an estimate that carries uncertainty. For a proportion such as accuracy p measured on n examples, the standard error is approximately:

So the statement “model B is 1 point better than A on 1,000 test cases” is usually not evidence of a real difference. Before declaring a winner, use confidence intervals, bootstrap resampling, or paired tests (McNemar's test for two classifiers on the same examples).

blocks.quote: A difference smaller than the confidence interval is not a win; it is noise until proven otherwise.

ul: **Null hypothesis:** “no difference”.
**p-value:** the probability of seeing a difference at least this large **if the null hypothesis were true** — not the probability that the new variant is better.
**Significance level of 0.05:** accepts a 5% false-positive rate per test.
**Statistical power** — commonly 80%: the probability of detecting a real effect of a given size; it determines the sample size.
Small effects need very large samples: detecting a rise in conversion from 5.0% to 5.5% needs tens of thousands of users in each arm.

blocks.p: A correct statement for p = 0.03: “If there were no real difference, a gap this large or larger would appear in about 3% of runs.” Options that say “there is a 97% probability that the new model is better” or “there is a 3% probability that the null hypothesis is true” are wrong.

blocks.p: **Correlation is not causation.** Observational data show associations confounded by other variables (ice-cream sales and drownings both rise in summer). **Simpson's paradox:** a trend present in every subgroup can reverse when the groups are combined, because their sizes differ — so always look at the slices.

Causal questions such as “did the retention campaign reduce churn?” need randomised experiments or causal-inference methods (difference-in-differences, propensity matching, uplift modelling), not just a predictive model.

With a disease prevalence of 1% and a test with 95% sensitivity and 95% specificity, a positive result means only about a 16% probability of disease, because the false positives from the healthy majority (99%) outnumber the true positives. Out of 10,000 people:

blocks.p: The best offline score is only one criterion. An expert engineer compares candidates on:

ul: Performance on critical slices.
Calibration.
Latency and memory at the required throughput.
Cost to train and serve.
Robustness to drift and noise.
The interpretability that regulation requires.
Maintenance burden (dependencies, retraining time).
Fairness.

blocks.quote: A model that is half a point better but ten times more expensive, opaque and slower than the SLA is the wrong choice — the same logic as in spec-matching questions.

blocks.p: **Ensembles** — averaging, stacking and blending — usually add a little accuracy at the price of latency, cost and complexity. They are worth it in competitions, and often not worth it in production unless the gain has business value.

blocks.p: Interpretability serves three audiences:

ul: **Developers:** debugging and leakage detection — a suspiciously dominant feature is often a leak.
**Regulators and auditors:** the Transparency & Explainability principle, and documentation.
**Affected individuals:** the reasons for a decision and a path to contest it.

blocks.quote: The more consequential the decision, the more the exam favours inherently interpretable models, or faithful local explanations with human review.

chapters.title: Metrics Worked Through with Numbers and Evaluation-Set Design

blocks.p: A fraud model is evaluated on 100,000 transactions, 500 of which are fraud. The model flags 1,250 transactions, of which 400 are actually fraud.

table: Looks excellent — and says almost nothing here
About 1 in 3 fraud alerts is real
4 out of every 5 frauds are caught
A tiny rate, but 850 customers were affected
A balanced view of precision and recall

blocks.quote: The “always predict legitimate” baseline has a higher overall accuracy than the useful model. Rates hide volumes: 0.85% means 850 reviews, and capacity questions are about volumes.

blocks.p: Lowering the threshold trades precision for recall. Which row is “best” depends on costs and capacity:

ul: Capacity of 3,000 reviews, and a missed fraud costs far more than a review → threshold **0.30** (2,800 alerts, 91% recall) is the best feasible operating point; 0.10 exceeds capacity (7,000).
Capacity of 700 reviews → threshold **0.70** (600 alerts) is the limit; 0.50 exceeds capacity (1,250).

blocks.quote: Same model, different correct thresholds — which is why the answer changes in scenarios where only the operational constraint changes.

ul: **Macro-F1** is the mean of the class F1 scores with equal weights — it exposes the failing rare classes.
**Weighted-F1** is the mean weighted by the number of cases — large classes dominate it, so it looks healthy.
**Micro metrics** pool all decisions and behave like overall accuracy.

blocks.p: If the rare classes are the ones that matter (legal threats, safety incidents), report Macro-F1 and per-class recall, and consider separate detectors for them or higher class weights.

ul: **MAE = 17 units:** the average miss, in the units of the target itself.
**RMSE ≈ 27.5:** inflated by the single large miss on day 4; use it when large errors are especially costly.
**MAPE:** undefined on day 5 (actual = 0) and explodes near zero — unsafe for intermittent demand.
**WAPE = 17%:** robust and easy to explain to the business.
**Bias = −11:** the model under-forecasts on average, which causes stock-outs.

blocks.p: A query has 3 relevant documents in the corpus. The system returns 5 results, and the relevant ones are at ranks 2 and 4.

blocks.formula: MRR = 1 / rank of first relevant = 1 / 2 = 0.50   (averaged over many queries)

blocks.p: nDCG rewards relevant results more the higher they are ranked, using a logarithmic discount (the document at rank i is divided by log₂(i+1)).

blocks.quote: In RAG, the retriever's Recall@k is usually the first metric to fix: if the right passage never reaches the model, no prompt can save the answer. Precision and ranking come after that, to reduce noise and tokens.

blocks.p: The ranking may be good (the higher bins default more), but probabilities above 10% are roughly double the observed rates — which is common after up-weighting the minority class. Good ranking (a high AUC) does not mean correct probabilities.
If these probabilities set interest rates or provisions, apply Platt scaling or isotonic calibration on a recent held-out period, and track the Brier score and a reliability curve over time.
An evaluation set is a specification written in data: it defines what “good” means, so it must be designed, not merely sampled.

ol: **Representative:** it matches the production population in channels, regions, dialects, devices and time; refresh it when the population changes.

**Stratified for what matters:** enough examples of rare but critical cases (fraud types, safety incidents, minority classes, unanswerable questions) to measure them with useful confidence, even if that means over-representing them relative to production; report both the overall figures and the per-slice figures.
**Clean labels:** labelled by experts following guidelines, with agreement measured; ambiguous cases are resolved or flagged.

**Isolated:** never used for training or tuning; access-controlled so that it does not leak into prompts or fine-tuning data; keep a development set for iteration separate from a test set that is rarely used.
**Versioned:** results are comparable only on the same version; record the version on which each model was evaluated.
**Linked to decisions:** each metric has a threshold agreed in advance (a release gate) and an owner.

blocks.p: These add: real user queries (anonymised), multi-turn conversations, adversarial prompts, questions that require refusal, dialect and mixed-language variants, and expected properties (must cite source X, must refuse, must ask a clarifying question) instead of single exact answers.

blocks.p: **Batch versus streaming for features:** streaming pipelines offer freshness in seconds but are harder to build, test and backfill. Use them only when freshness changes the decision (fraud, real-time personalisation); otherwise batch is cheaper and more reliable. The common hybrid pattern: long-window features computed in batch alongside a few short-window streaming features, all served from the connected feature store.
**Reproducibility:** every training run must point to a fixed data snapshot (table version, file fingerprints) together with the code version (commit) and the parameters.

blocks.quote: “We cannot reproduce last quarter's model” is a governance failure: auditors, incident investigations and PDPL deletion requests all depend on knowing exactly which data the model saw.

sections.title: 4.3 The Multi-Stage Search and Recommendation Funnel

blocks.p: Search and recommendation appear in e-commerce, media, government portals and internal knowledge bases. Both follow a multi-stage funnel: retrieve a few hundred candidates cheaply from millions of items, then rank them with a stronger model, then apply business rules.

table: ANN over user/item embeddings, co-visitation, most popular in the region
Learning-to-rank or a cross-encoder on query–document features
Boosted trees or a neural ranker on user, item and context features
Diversity, novelty, stock availability, compliance, fairness to sellers

sections.title: 4.4 Feedback, Cold Start, Arabic Search and Metrics

blocks.p: **Feedback and bias:** users click only on what was shown, and they click the top positions more (position bias). Naive training on clicks reinforces whatever the current system displays. The remedy:

ul: Log impressions together with their positions.
Use counterfactual training or a position-bias corrector.
Reserve a small share of traffic for exploration.
Validate with A/B tests on business outcomes (conversion, satisfaction, retention), not on click-through rate alone.

blocks.p: **Cold start:** new items gain exposure through content embeddings and exploration slots; new users get “most popular in their segment” recommendations and the preferences they give at onboarding.

**Arabic search specifics:** normalisation (the forms of alef, yaa and taa marbuta, and diacritics), light stemming or morphological analysis for keyword search, synonyms and dialectal forms (different names for the same product between regions), literal transliteration of brand names, and queries that mix Arabic and English. Hybrid search is usually the strongest baseline.

table: Recall@k for candidate generation; nDCG/MRR for ranking
Click-through and conversion rates, and also the zero-result rate, the query-reformulation rate, time to success and long-term retention
Specific slices: Arabic versus English queries, new versus returning users

lab.purpose: Apply calculation, statistics and model selection to a real decision: should we replace the current credit-scoring model with a new one? At what threshold, and with what safeguards?
scenario: A Saudi financing company uses logistic regression to score personal-finance applications. The data science team proposed a stacking ensemble of three boosted-tree models that achieved an AUC of 0.842, against 0.836 for the current model, on a test set of 1,000 applications; its latency is 180 ms against an SLA of 100 ms. The team trained the new model with up-weighting of the defaulter class.

When calibration was checked, the observed default rate in the 20–40% probability bin was about 14%, and in the 40%+ bin about 31%. The probabilities are used directly to set the profit margin. The team also ran a small A/B test on the app channel; it checked the results daily and stopped on day 4, when p = 0.04 appeared on one metric out of the 15 being monitored, and the actual split between the two arms was 53/47 although the design was 50/50.
steps: Estimate the uncertainty: a difference of 0.006 in AUC on 1,000 examples is not sufficient evidence of superiority — for comparison, a proportion near 0.90 measured on 1,000 examples carries a confidence interval of about ±1.9 points on its own. Calculate a confidence interval for the AUC difference by bootstrap resampling on the same examples before making any claim.

Evaluate the candidates on criteria beyond the leaderboard: the new model violates the latency SLA, is more opaque and more complex, and its gain is unproven — so it is the wrong choice by the logic of spec matching.

Read the calibration: the probabilities are roughly double the observed rates above 10%, which is expected after up-weighting the minority class. If either model is used for pricing, apply Platt or isotonic calibration on a recent held-out period and monitor the Brier score and a reliability curve.

Reject the A/B test result: peeking and early stopping inflate false positives; 15 metrics at 0.05 produce an expected false win; the sample ratio mismatch (53/47) means a broken assignment that must be investigated before reading anything; and 4 days is less than one full weekly cycle.

Redesign the experiment: a primary metric fixed in advance, a sample size calculated for 80% power, a duration of at least one or two weekly cycles, and a correction for multiple comparisons on the secondary metrics.

Check regulatory compliance: credit is a high-impact decision, so keep an interpretable model, or boosted trees with monotonic constraints and faithful reason codes (SHAP), fairness by group and human review; and remember that the training data contains selection bias (outcomes are known only for approved loans).
Fix the evaluation set: a specific version, critical slices with sufficient representation, and a release gate agreed in advance for each metric, with an owner.
traps: Treating a small difference in AUC or accuracy on 1,000 examples as evidence of superiority without confidence intervals.
Interpreting p = 0.04 as “a 96% probability that the new model is better”.
Choosing the highest-scoring ensemble despite its violation of latency, interpretability and cost.
Confusing ranking quality (AUC) with the correctness of the probabilities (calibration) when the probabilities are used for pricing.
Calculating MAPE for intermittent demand that contains zeros, or reporting Weighted-F1 when the rare classes are the ones that matter.
Choosing a threshold that produces more alerts than the available review capacity.
lab.deliverable: A decision documented with numbers: keep the current model with calibration, or rerun a correctly designed experiment, with statistical, operational and regulatory justification for every step.

review.q: Tabular churn data with half a million rows. What is the strong default choice, and why?
review.a: Boosted trees (XGBoost/LightGBM/CatBoost): the best available for tabular data, they handle missing values, and they have fast inference on CPU. Deep networks do not usually win on this type of data.

review.q: A model has 90% accuracy on 100 test examples. What is the approximate 95% confidence interval?
review.a: The standard error is √(0.9×0.1/100) = 0.03, so the confidence interval is about ±5.9 points. Any difference smaller than that between two models on this set is not evidence.

review.q: What is the correct interpretation of the p-value p = 0.03 in an A/B test?
review.a: If there were no real difference, a gap this large or larger would appear in about 3% of runs. It is not the probability that the new variant is better, nor the probability that the null hypothesis is true.

review.q: A disease has a prevalence of 1%, and the test has 95% sensitivity and 95% specificity. What is the probability of disease given a positive result?
review.a: Only about 16%: out of 10,000 people, there are 95 true positives against 495 false positives from the healthy majority. This is why precision is low in rare-event detection.

review.q: From a confusion matrix: TP=400, FP=850, FN=100, TN=98,650. Calculate precision, recall and F1.
review.a: Precision is 400/1,250 = 32%, recall is 400/500 = 80%, and F1 = 2×0.32×0.80/1.12 ≈ 0.457. The overall accuracy of 99.05% is lower than the “never fraud” baseline (99.5%).

review.q: The review team's capacity is 700 alerts, and the available thresholds produce 300, 600 and 1,250 alerts at 0.90, 0.70 and 0.50. Which threshold?
review.a: 0.70: the lowest threshold that does not exceed capacity, giving 66% recall against 48% at 0.90. The 0.50 threshold produces 1,250 alerts, which exceeds capacity.

review.q: Why was Macro-F1 ≈ 0.638 while Weighted-F1 ≈ 0.930 in the customer-service ticket example?
review.a: Weighted-F1 is dominated by the large classes (billing and network), so it looks healthy, whereas Macro-F1 gives every class the same weight and so exposes the weakness of the legal-threat class (0.400) and the safety-incident class (0.286).

review.q: Why is WAPE preferred to MAPE when forecasting demand that has days with no sales?
review.a: MAPE is undefined when the actual value is zero and explodes near it, whereas WAPE = sum of absolute errors ÷ sum of actuals (85/500 = 17% in the example) is robust and easy to explain to the business.

review.q: In a RAG system, which retriever metric do you fix first?
review.a: Recall@k: if the right passage never reaches the model, no prompt can save the answer. After that, precision and ranking (nDCG, MRR) are improved to reduce noise and tokens.

review.q: An A/B test designed as 50/50 produced a 52/48 split. What do you do?
review.a: This is a sample ratio mismatch, which indicates a broken assignment mechanism; investigate and fix it before reading any result, because the comparison itself is no longer reliable.

summary: You have mastered this unit when you can name the right family for any scenario together with its weakness, from which a distractor may be built; calculate every metric from the confusion matrix, the error tables and the ranking without hesitation; choose the feasible threshold within capacity; reject a “win” that is smaller than the confidence interval or that comes from peeking and multiple comparisons; prefer the model that meets latency, interpretability and cost over the one with the highest score; and then design a representative, isolated evaluation set, reproducible data pipelines, a search and recommendation funnel, and time-series forecasts that are evaluated forward in time and whose decisions are built on quantiles.
